title: What I've Been Learning Recently: AI That Understands More Than Text
description: A look at EmbeddingGemma 2, why text, images, audio and video can share an embedding space, and what this means for practical AI search.
body:
I’ve been reading about a new kind of embedding model, and it made me rethink something I’d taken for granted about search.

Usually, when we talk about search in AI, we imagine typing a question, turning it into a vector, and finding the nearest matching chunks of text. That works well for documentation. But real information doesn’t live only in paragraphs. It’s in screenshots, diagrams, voice recordings, code, and videos too.

That’s what caught my attention about **EmbeddingGemma 2**, which Google DeepMind released on October 6, 2026. It’s an open multimodal embedding model designed to place different types of content in a shared space, so they can be searched by *meaning*, not just by format.

## First, what exactly is an embedding?

I like to think of an embedding as a location on a map that you can’t see.

Instead of storing a sentence as words alone, a model represents its meaning as a list of numbers called a vector. Items with related meanings should end up closer together. You don’t need the exact same wording to find something useful.

The interesting part is extending that idea beyond text. What if a sentence describing a dog running through a park could sit near a photo or video showing that scene? Suddenly, a typed query could help retrieve a visual moment too.

[[sketch:modalities]]

## The new part: one shared space for different media

EmbeddingGemma 2 handles **text and code, images, audio, and video**. It uses specialized components for some of those inputs, but the resulting representations can be compared in a common **768-dimensional embedding space**.

That matters because the usual alternative is to maintain separate systems for separate formats—or convert everything into text first, which may lose visual and acoustic details.

The model’s full multimodal configuration has **740 million parameters**. Its text portion accounts for about **270 million**, with optional vision and audio encoders contributing the rest. Google designed those components to be loaded selectively instead of forcing every application to carry all of them.

One detail I found especially interesting: audio can be embedded directly, without always needing a speech-to-text transcript first. That creates possibilities for searching sounds and recordings based on what they contain, not just words somebody said.

## How would the search actually work?

Here’s a simplified way I understand the process.

- **Step 1:** Put your documents, images, recordings, or video clips through the appropriate embedding path.
- **Step 2:** Save the vectors in a searchable index, along with references to the original content.
- **Step 3:** Turn a user’s question into an embedding in that same space.
- **Step 4:** Compare the vectors, retrieve the closest relevant items, and show the actual source. If you're building a RAG assistant, pass those retrieved items to a generation model with citations.

[[sketch:pipeline]]

The embedding model is **not** the chatbot and it doesn’t write the final answer. Its job is retrieval: helping the application locate useful evidence. That distinction seems small, but it changes how I think about designing an AI product.

Imagine asking, “Where did I explain the graph database?” and getting back a timestamp from a demo video, a relevant diagram, and a page from the documentation. That’s the kind of experience a multimodal retrieval pipeline could support. It is an example of what I would like to experiment with, not something I’ve benchmarked myself.

## The engineering trade-off I liked most

The other thing worth learning here is **Matryoshka Representation Learning**.

EmbeddingGemma 2 produces 768-dimensional vectors by default, but developers can also use shorter representations such as **512, 256, or 128 dimensions**. Fewer dimensions mean less vector data to store and potentially less work when searching a large collection.

That sounds like an easy win, but there’s a trade-off. Compressing the representation can reduce retrieval quality, especially for certain modalities or difficult queries.

Google’s model card also points out an implementation detail I don’t want to miss: if you truncate a vector manually, you should normalize it again before computing cosine similarity. Queries and stored vectors also need to use the same dimensionality.

[[sketch:dimensions]]

I find this more useful than a vague promise of “faster AI.” It gives an engineer a measurable decision to make: which vector size gives acceptable search quality for the memory and latency budget?

## Where I'd try this

If I were evaluating it in a project, I’d start small: a mixed collection of architecture notes, screenshots, short demos, and code snippets.

I’d then test questions that are easy for text search, plus questions that *require* a visual or audio clue. I would compare retrieval relevance, storage size, indexing time, and search latency at different dimensions.

There’s also a practical question: how do you chunk or sample a long video so the most useful moment can be retrieved? And how do you keep permissions and citations attached to the original source? A shared embedding space helps, but it doesn’t solve the rest of the application by itself.

## What I'm taking away

The biggest shift for me is this: an AI search system doesn’t have to treat every file type as a separate island.

EmbeddingGemma 2 is interesting because it brings text, code, visual content, and audio closer together in a model intended for everyday hardware. It’s not a substitute for good evaluation, careful data handling, or a reliable retrieval pipeline. But it’s a building block I want to understand better.

Sometimes the most exciting AI advances aren't another chatbot feature. They're the less visible pieces that make better products possible.
